{{short description|American mathematician|bot=PearBOT 5}}
'''Woodrow Dale Brownawell''' (born April 21, 1942) is an American [[mathematician]] who has performed research in [[number theory]] and [[algebraic geometry]]. He is a Distinguished Professor emeritus at [[Pennsylvania State University]],<ref name="cv">[http://www.math.psu.edu/wdb/CV.html Curriculum vitae], retrieved January 25, 2015.</ref> and is particularly known for his proof of explicit degree bounds that can be used to turn [[Hilbert's Nullstellensatz]] into an effective [[algorithm]].<ref name="faces"/><ref>{{citation
 | last = Smale | first = Stephen | authorlink = Stephen Smale
 | contribution = On problems of computational complexity
 | doi = 10.1017/CBO9780511614156.012
 | mr = 2166931
 | pages = 255–259
 | publisher = Cambridge Univ. Press, Cambridge
 | series = London Math. Soc. Lecture Note Ser.
 | title = Surveys in modern mathematics
 | volume = 321
 | year = 2005 | isbn = 978-0-521-54793-2 }}.</ref>

Brownawell was born in [[Grundy County, Missouri]];<ref name="cv"/> his father was a farmer and train inspector.<ref name="faces">{{citation|title=Faces of Penn State, 2005: W. Dale Brownawell, Distinguished Professor of Mathematics|url=http://science.psu.edu/journal/Summer2005/BrownawellSum05.htm|publisher=Penn State Eberly College of Science|year=2005|access-date=January 25, 2015|first=Suzan|last=Erem}}.</ref> He earned a double baccalaureate in [[German language|German]] and mathematics (with highest distinction) in 1964 from the [[University of Kansas]],<ref name="cv"/> and after studying for a year at the [[University of Hamburg]]<ref name="cv"/> (at which he met Eva, the woman he later married)<ref name="faces"/> he returned to the US for graduate study at [[Cornell University]].<ref name="cv"/> His graduate advisor, [[Stephen Schanuel]], moved to [[Stony Brook University]] in 1969, and Brownawell followed him there for a year,<ref name="cv"/> but earned his Ph.D. from Cornell in 1970.<ref name="cv"/><ref>{{mathgenealogy|id=40299}}</ref> That year, he joined the Penn State faculty, and he remained there until his retirement in 2013.<ref name="cv"/>

Brownawell and [[Michel Waldschmidt]] shared the 1986 Hardy–Ramanujan Prize for their independent proofs that at least one of the two numbers <math>e^e</math> and <math>e^{e^2}</math> is a [[transcendental number]]; here <math>e</math> denotes [[e (mathematical constant)|Euler's number]], approximately 2.718.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Waldschmidt | first = Michel | authorlink = Michel Waldschmidt
 | journal = Hardy-Ramanujan Journal
 | mr = 1680117
 | title = On the numbers <math>e^e</math>, <math>e^{e^2}</math> and <math>e^{\pi^2}</math>
 | url = https://www.imj-prg.fr/~michel.waldschmidt/articles/ps/HRJ.ps
 | volume = 21
 | year = 1998}}.</ref>
In 2004, a conference at the [[University of Waterloo]] was held in honor of Brownawell's 60th birthday.<ref>[http://www.fields.utoronto.ca/programs/scientific/03-04/brownawell/ The Brownawell Conference, In celebration of the 60th birthday of W.Dale Brownawell, June 17-19, 2004], [[Fields Institute]], retrieved January 25, 2015.</ref>
In 2012, he became one of the inaugural [[fellow]]s of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180825194636/http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list |date=August 25, 2018 }}, retrieved January 25, 2015.</ref>
